dialogs.title: Dialogue — Eczanede
dialogs.intro: Budi walks into the pharmacy near home. His voice is hoarse and his nose is red.

lines.speaker: Eczacı:
lines.id: Hello, how can I help you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm not well. I think I've got the flu.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Boğazım ağrıyor ve başım ağrıyor. Ateşim de var.
lines.id: My throat hurts and I have a headache. I have a fever too.
lines.literal: throat-my aches and head-my aches. fever-my too there-is.

lines.speaker: Eczacı:
lines.id: How many days has it been like this?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: İki gündür. Dün gece hiç uyuyamadım.
lines.id: Two days. Last night I couldn't sleep at all.
lines.literal: two day-for. yesterday night at-all couldn't-sleep-I.

lines.speaker: Eczacı:
lines.text: Alerjin var mı? İlaç kullanıyor musun?
lines.id: Do you have any allergies? Are you taking any medicine?
lines.literal: allergy-your there-is question? medicine using question-you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I have no allergies, and I'm not taking any medicine.

lines.speaker: Eczacı:
lines.text: Bu ağrı kesici, günde iki kere. Bu da boğaz için pastil.
lines.id: This is a painkiller, twice a day. And these are throat lozenges.

lines.speaker: Eczacı:
lines.text: Yemekten sonra. Bol su iç ve dinlen. İki gün geçmezse doktora git.
lines.id: After meals. Drink plenty of water and rest. If it's not better in two days, go to a doctor.

notes: **Geçmiş olsun is said to anyone who is sick or just recovering** — also after an accident, a tough exam or a minor misfortune. Literally "may it be over". The reply is *teşekkür ederim*.

**Neyin var? is literally "what do you have?"** — the Turkish way to ask about symptoms. The answer uses the same pattern: *ateşim var* (I have a fever), *başım ağrıyor*, *midem bulanıyor* (I feel sick).

**Grip oldum, not gribim.** For an illness that HAPPENS to you, use *olmak*: *grip oldum* (I've caught the flu), *hasta oldum* (I got sick). For an ongoing state, use the ordinary person ending: *hastayım* (I'm sick).
**Kaç gündür** uses the suffix *-dır*, meaning "for, since": *iki gündür* (for two days), *bir haftadır* (for a week), *yıllardır* (for years). It's very common and easy to learn as a whole.

blocks.text: Some of these words drop a vowel as soon as a suffix is added: *burun → burnum* (my nose), *ağız → ağzım*, *karın → karnım*, *boyun → boynum*. The same pattern as *oğul → oğlum* in unit 4.

blocks.title: Dil means two things
items: *Dil* is both "tongue" and "language" — just like English "mother tongue" and Arabic *lisan*. *Türk dili* = the Turkish language. *Dilim yandı* = I burned my tongue.
The word *göz* does double duty too: besides "eye", it means "drawer" and "compartment". *Gözlük* (glasses) is literally "eye gear".

blocks.text: The pattern is always the same: **body part + possessive suffix + ağrıyor**. Turkish doesn't say "I have a headache" but "my head is aching".
*Başım dönüyor* is literally "my head is spinning" — exactly the same image as in English. Languages often agree without ever having met.

blocks.title: Nöbetçi eczane
items: Pharmacies in Turkey close at night, but every district always has one on duty — the *nöbetçi eczane*. The list is posted on the door of every closed pharmacy, and you can find it online.

Many medicines sold over the counter elsewhere need a *reçete* (prescription) in Turkey. Turkish pharmacists are well trained and used to advising on minor complaints — they're the first stop, not the doctor.
